newsitem.title: USA: Early pickup for shuttle satellite - NASA.
newsitem.headline: Early pickup for shuttle satellite - NASA.

text.p: The space shuttle will pick up a prototype space factory slightly earlier than planned so a space observatory does not stray too close to it, NASA officials said on Sunday
The Wake Shield Facility, released from Columbia on Friday night, will be picked up on Monday at 9:11 p.m., about three hours earlier than originally planned.
"We will be retrieving it two orbits early," spacecraft communicator Marc Garneau told the shuttle crew on Sunday.

NASA officials had earlier considered moving up the satellite recovery by a day, but improved tracking revealed the Orfeus-Spas telescope, deployed by the shuttle last Tuesday, would be just far enough away for the shuttle to make a safe approach later.
The pair are expected to be 13 miles apart when Columbia swoops in to collect the Wake Shield. The craft must be separated by at least 12.5 miles, shuttle flight director Rob Kelso said.
Flight controllers at NASA's mission control in Houston called up military tracking radars to get a better fix on the location of the two satellites.

"We've been spending most of our time ... crunching the computer in the control centre to predict the flight path of the Spas and the Wake Shield ... to answer the question who is going to be where when," Kelso told a news conference.
The saucer-shaped Wake Shield was designed to manufacture ultra-pure semiconductors for the electronics industry. They could lead to faster computer chips and better, smaller cellular phones.

NASA believes the two spacecraft drew unexpectedly close when the Orfeus-Spas telescope encountered more drag than expected from the thin upper atmosphere 220 miles (355 km) up as it was pointed at its celestial targets.

The telescope ceased observations on Sunday afternoon so it could be oriented to reduce the braking effect of the atmosphere. The telescope was not expected to resume work until Monday morning at the earliest.
This mission of the shuttle marks the first time NASA has flown it in formation with two recoverable satellites. Flight director Al Pennington said before the mission the task would be "tricky."
The decision not to retrieve the Wake Shield a day early will allow it to complete its seventh and final semiconductor manufacturing run.
The five astronauts, who are one-third of the way through a 16-day mission, took six hours off duty on Sunday and made private phone calls to their families.
